query: For additively manufactured high-entropy-alloy components, what single intervention could improve dimensional precision and mechanical integrity while reducing fabrication-induced defects? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to the current fabrication baseline, defines the processing and application conditions under which it should hold, identifies supporting prior evidence, and proposes an experiment whose result would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Applying an in‐situ periodic laser remelting step immediately after each layer is deposited will act to reflow the material, homogenize thermal gradients, and reduce residual stresses, thereby improving dimensional accuracy, reducing fabrication‐induced defects, and enhancing the mechanical integrity of additively manufactured high-entropy alloy components.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured CoCrFeNiMn high-entropy alloy component produced via standard SLM processing that exhibits dimensional deviations (warpage, shrinkage) and residual defects (microcracking, porosity) due to rapid solidification.
generation.intervention: In-situ, secondary laser remelting of each deposited layer using an optimized laser pass immediately after layer deposition.
generation.conditions: Use the same build material (e.g., CoCrFeNiMn HEA) and baseline SLM parameters (laser power, scan speed, layer thickness, etc.) as in conventional builds; incorporate an additional remelting pass with energy input tuned to reflow the just-deposited layer without keyholing, all under standard inert atmosphere and controlled build platform temperature.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined microstructural features with reduced thermal gradients and lower interlayer residual stresses; improved metallurgical bonding across layers.
generation.mechanism: The additional in-situ remelting pass re-melts the top portion of each layer, effectively reducing sharp temperature differentials and the associated residual stress. This homogenization minimizes local overcooling‐induced shrinkage and microcrack formation, leading to a component with tighter dimensional tolerances and enhanced mechanical integrity.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to standard SLM processing, components subjected to periodic in-situ laser remelting are expected to show a measurable reduction (on the order of approximately 15–20%) in dimensional deviations (warpage/shrinkage) and lower defect densities (microcracks and porosity), as well as improved tensile strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: Standard SLM-fabricated high-entropy alloy components produced without any post-deposition remelting steps, which are known to suffer from residual stress accumulation, microstructural anisotropy, and associated dimensional inaccuracies.
generation.boundary: This intervention is expected to be effective for HEA systems with thermal properties similar to CoCrFeNiMn and under SLM conditions where rapid solidification leads to significant residual stress. Its benefits might be diminished or require parameter reoptimization for alloys with very different melting points or thermal conductivities, or for geometrically complex components where remelting could induce additional distortion.
generation.uncertainty: This proposal builds on the laser remelting findings from the Al0.65CoCrFeNi study (PMC9919236::web::000::abstract) which demonstrated surface microstructural refinement, and on the crack-mitigation insights from thermal management strategies in CrNbTiZr alloy processing (PMC12348559::web::019::4_discussion). What is new here is the systematic application of in-situ remelting specifically targeting dimensional precision and overall defect reduction. However, the quantitative improvement, optimal remelting parameters, and possible side effects (e.g., inadvertent over-melting or changes in microstructure that might compromise other properties) remain uncertain.

falsification_experiment.design: Produce two sets of identical components via SLM using a high-entropy alloy such as CoCrFeNiMn. One set will be fabricated using the standard SLM process while the other will include an optimized in-situ laser remelting pass after each layer. Both sets will be produced under otherwise identical processing conditions.
measurements: Dimensional accuracy assessment using high-precision coordinate measurement machines (CMM) to quantify deviations (warpage, shrinkage).
Residual stress measurement via X-ray diffraction or in-situ stress sensors.
Defect density evaluation by non-destructive techniques (e.g., CT scanning) and detailed SEM analysis.
Mechanical performance testing including tensile and fatigue tests to compare strength and ductility.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the in-situ remelted components do not show a statistically significant (approximately >15%) reduction in dimensional deviations and residual defect density, accompanied by improvements in mechanical properties, as compared to the standard SLM components, the hypothesis will be considered falsified.

LMD–DCT has been proven to be an effective method of synergistically improving the strength and plasticity of the alloy. Furthermore, DCT with a long immersion time can avoid a large degree of processing deformation and directly promote the formation of HCP precipitates near the grain boundary position. The presence of precipitates further improves the strength of the alloy. The DCT method can effectively utilize the residual stress accumulated in the alloy during the forming process of laser additive manufacturing methods such as LMD. Compared with traditional rolling methods, the DCT method is more suitable for the modification of complex shape parts formed by LMD near-net forming. For HfNbTaTiZr alloy, DCT can also be targeted for phase control. It can be said that DCT is an excellent supporting scheme for additive manufacturing. The present study demonstrates that a strategic combination of deposition-parameters optimization and thermal management enables the fabrication of a crack-free bulk CrNbTiZr RCCA via L-DED using elemental powders. This represents a significant advancement, as prior efforts involving DED of similar systems have typically been limited to thin-wall geometries and have often suffered from severe cracking, substantial residual porosity, or incomplete fusion [,,,,,,]. Our results indicate that insulating the build platform and minimizing the dwell time between the layers elevates the overall temperature of the sample, effectively preventing the formation of macrocracks. It can be attributed to the fact that the deposition on insulated substrate reduces temperature gradients created at the edge of the melt pool which in turn decreases the strain concentrations and suppresses the formation of cracks. In contrast, samples deposited on the thermally conductive platform exhibited pronounced cracking. A laser-induced pre-heating temperature of approximately 500 °C was determined to be adequate to achieve this effect.

It should be noted that the effect of SLM additive manufacturing microstructure anisotropy on fatigue performance is also considered. Various metal structures suitable for SLM manufacturing are comparable to their casting and forging materials in quasi-static strength. Still, their fracture toughness is generally low, and the discrete characteristics of fatigue performance test data are significant, which is not only related to process defects but also significantly related to the characteristics of the SLM microstructure. The laser remelting technique was applied to the surface modification of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) to further advance its mechanical potential. The microstructure of the remelted layer was refined from coarse dendritic to submicron-scale basket weave compared with the as-cast substrate, resulting in a 1.8-time increase in Vickers microhardness. The nanoindentation tests indicated that the nanohardness of the remelted layer was higher than that of each phase in the substrate. Meanwhile, the remelted layer retained considerable plasticity, as evidenced by its high Wp/Wt ratio (0.763) and strain hardening exponent (0.302). Additionally, adhesive wear prevailed on the substrate, while only abrasive wear features were observed on the remelted layer. Accordingly, the average friction coefficient and the wear rate of the remelted layer were minimized by 23% and 80%, respectively, compared with the substrate. Our findings explored an industrialized method to enhance the surface properties of the Al0.65CoCrFeNi HEA and also provided some helpful references for its laser additive manufacturing.
